summary: An introductory guide to TCP/IP and Internet tools and utilities that let users reach information on the network, from checking whether a host is up to browsing documents. It also covers discussion lists. It was replaced by RFC 2151.

eli5.summary: A beginner's toolbox guide for exploring the early internet.

questions: how to use ftp telnet ping
subtitle: A beginner's guide to TCP/IP utilities and Internet tools

tldr.problem: Early Internet users had many tools available (PING, FTP, TELNET, WHOIS, ARCHIE, GOPHER) but lacked a comprehensive guide that explained what each tool did, how to use it, and when to use it. Different implementations had different interfaces, making it hard for newcomers to navigate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1739 provides a tutorial guide with descriptions and sample sessions for each major TCP/IP tool, shows how to use discussion lists and mailing lists, explains how to find and retrieve Internet documents, and includes an acronyms glossary.
tldr.outcome: The guide helped newcomers learn early Internet tools and practice using them. It was replaced by RFC 2151 as newer tools and updated usage patterns emerged.

today: RFC 1739 is historic and was obsoleted by RFC 2151. Many of the tools described (ARCHIE, Gopher, FINGER, TELNET) are rarely used today, having been replaced by web browsers, search engines, and modern applications. However, some tools like DNS lookups, PING, FTP, and the concept of mailing lists remain in use, though with different interfaces and implementations.

sections.title: Overview of TCP/IP Tools
sections.content:
RFC 1739 is an introductory guide to TCP/IP utilities and Internet tools that let users reach information and services on the network. The document acknowledges that while the TCP/IP protocol suite is powerful, the tools available have different interfaces depending on the operating system and software package. This guide aims to teach newcomers what each tool does, show sample sessions with actual command-line examples, and help them understand when and how to use them.

The RFC is designed as a tutorial for self-learning, a laboratory manual for courses, or a basis for site user manuals. It emphasizes that this is a basic guide; users needing detailed information are referred to RFCs, technical reports, and books on TCP/IP. The guide covers tools that worked with VAX/VMS, DOS, UNIX, and other systems available in the early 1990s, though exact command syntax varied across platforms.
sections.eli5: This is a guide to all the main Internet tools from the early 1990s. It explains what each tool does and shows examples of using them.

sections.title: Essential Utilities
sections.content:
The RFC covers several core utilities that come with most TCP/IP implementations. NSLOOKUP allows users to query the Domain Name System (DNS) to find IP addresses and hostnames, and can retrieve other DNS records like mail exchange (MX) records. PING uses ICMP Echo messages to test if a remote host is reachable and measure response time. FINGER lets users look up information about users on remote systems and see who is currently logged in.

TRACEROUTE shows the path that data packets take from your computer to a remote host, listing each router (hop) along the route and measuring response times. This is useful for understanding network topology and debugging routing problems. The RFC includes a detailed sample showing packets traveling from a regional network to the national backbone and then to a destination, illustrating how networks are interconnected.

FTP (File Transfer Protocol) lets users upload and download files to remote computers, with anonymous FTP allowing public access without a password. TELNET provides remote terminal access, allowing a user to log into another computer and run commands there, including access to special services on non-standard ports.
sections.eli5: NSLOOKUP finds computers by name, PING checks if they're online, FINGER looks up people, TRACEROUTE shows the path your messages take, and FTP and TELNET let you get files and log in remotely.

sections.title: Directory and Lookup Services
sections.content:
WHOIS (also called NICNAME) searches databases to find network administrators, RFC authors, domain contacts, and registered individuals. The InterNIC database contains Internet domains and IP network information. Other WHOIS servers cover MILNET and other networks. KNOWBOT is an automated search tool that queries multiple WHOIS databases simultaneously (InterNIC, MILNET, MCImail, PSI) to find people on the Internet.

NETFIND is another people-finding tool that uses FINGER and SMTP to locate users without relying on centralized databases. It is accessed via TELNET to a NETFIND server and provides a menu-driven interface. The RFC notes that NETFIND is newer and its use is growing as system administrators configure their servers to respond to NETFIND queries.
sections.eli5: WHOIS finds domain registrations and network contacts. KNOWBOT searches multiple directories at once. NETFIND searches the network itself to find people.

sections.title: Information Retrieval Systems
sections.content:
ARCHIE is a tool for locating files at anonymous FTP archive sites. The Archie server at McGill University (and mirrors worldwide) tracks the contents of over 1,000 FTP sites containing over 2 million files, updating monthly. Users access Archie via TELNET, logging in as 'archie', and use the prog command to search for files and whatis to search program descriptions. The RFC provides a list of Archie servers worldwide.

GOPHER, developed at the University of Minnesota, is a menu-driven, hierarchical information system that presents files and links in an organized menu structure. Users can browse menus, view files on demand, and link to other Gopher sites. Gopher is easier to use than Archie or command-line FTP because the menu structure is intuitive. TELNET access is available at many Gopher sites with username 'gopher'. Local Gopher client software is also available, making access even simpler.
sections.eli5: ARCHIE finds files at FTP sites. GOPHER presents Internet information in easy-to-navigate menus.

sections.title: Discussion Lists and Documentation
sections.content:
The RFC describes Internet discussion lists and mailing lists, where users join ongoing conversations about specific topics. These lists are accessible via LISTSERV software (which automates list administration) or through human-maintained lists. Usenet News (also called Network News) is a separate but parallel bulletin-board system with thousands of discussion groups organized in a hierarchy (comp.* for computers, rec.* for recreation, sci.* for science, soc.* for social topics, etc.). Usenet messages are distributed across the network, with each site carrying the groups its users are interested in.

The RFC also explains how to find and retrieve Internet documentation. RFCs (Request for Comments) are the document series describing Internet protocols and standards, available from multiple FTP repositories. FYI (For Your Information) documents are a subseries of RFCs for informational and introductory topics. Internet Standards are the subset of RFCs that describe official protocols. The guide explains how to use FTP and electronic mail to retrieve RFCs and other documents.
sections.eli5: People discuss topics in mailing lists and Usenet News. Internet documentation (RFCs and guides) is available for download via FTP or email.
